title: Rise of Mesoamerican civilization
summary: The Olmec of Mexico's Gulf lowlands were one of the earliest complex societies of ancient Mesoamerica. San Lorenzo, occupied from about 1500 BCE, flourished between 1200 and 850 BCE and left 129 stone monuments, including ten colossal heads. Olmec influence and trade spread from 1200 BCE as far south as present-day Nicaragua. Scholars still debate whether the Olmec were a mother culture for later Mesoamerica.

uncertainty.note: Encyclopedia.com dates initial occupation at the premier Early Formative capital of San Lorenzo to about 1500 BCE with peak prosperity 1200–850 BCE; World History Encyclopedia dates the Olmec civilization from c. 1200 BCE to c. 400 BCE.

as_recorded.value: Initial occupation from about 1500 bce was followed by its florescence, dated between 1200 and 850 bce
prospered in Pre-Classical (Formative) Mesoamerica from c. 1200 BCE to c. 400 BCE

where.historical_name: San Lorenzo, Coatzacoalcos river basin, southern Veracruz (Early Formative Olmec political and ceremonial center)

importance.justification: The Early Formative emergence of Olmec monumental architecture, elite governance, and ritual cosmology created the cultural template for all later Mesoamerican civilizations.

related.because: San Lorenzo served as the premier Early Formative capital and ceremonial center during the rise of Mesoamerican civilization.
Early ballcourt construction at Paso de la Amada reflects the emergence of public ceremonial architecture during the Formative period.
